installation.note: man is built-in on most Linux distributions by default

overview.summary: man (manual) displays system manual pages - the traditional Unix documentation system. Manual pages provide comprehensive documentation for commands, system calls, library functions, and configuration files. They're organized into sections (man pages).

misconceptions.title: man pages are hard to read
misconceptions.misconception: man pages are too technical and difficult for beginners
misconceptions.reality: Man pages are comprehensive but can be intimidating. They use standard navigation (arrow keys, / to search, q to quit). Start with SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION sections.
misconceptions.tip: Use arrow keys, / to search, q to quit. Start with SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION - skip to EXAMPLES if available.

misconceptions.title: man only shows command help
misconceptions.misconception: man only displays help for commands
misconceptions.reality: man pages document commands, system calls, library functions, file formats, and more. Organized into sections: 1=commands, 2=system calls, 3=functions, 5=files, 8=admin.
misconceptions.tip: man pages cover many things: commands (section 1), system calls (2), file formats (5), etc.

common_pitfalls.issue: Not knowing how to navigate man pages
common_pitfalls.description: Getting stuck in man page viewer
common_pitfalls.solution: Use arrow keys to scroll, /pattern to search, n for next match, N for previous, q to quit, h for help. Man pages use less pager.

common_pitfalls.description: Getting wrong man page when name exists in multiple sections
common_pitfalls.solution: Specify section: man 1 passwd (command) vs man 5 passwd (file format). Use man -k to search first.

common_pitfalls.description: Command not found in man pages
common_pitfalls.solution: Some commands are shell builtins (cd, history) - use help cd instead. Or install man pages: sudo apt install manpages

related_commands.relationship: Alternative documentation; info pages vs man pages
related_commands.description: Display info documentation (alternative to man pages, more detailed)

related_commands.relationship: Built-in help; help for shell builtins, man for external commands
related_commands.description: Help for shell built-in commands (cd, history, etc. - use help not man)

related_commands.relationship: Quick help; --help for quick reference, man for full docs
related_commands.description: Quick help flag available on most commands (ls --help)

best_practices: Use man command for detailed documentation
Use man -k keyword to search for commands by topic
Use arrow keys, / to search, q to quit in man pages
Start with SYNOPSIS and DESCRIPTION sections
Use man -f for quick one-line description
Specify section when needed: man 1 command vs man 5 command
performance_tips: Use man -f for fast one-line descriptions
Navigation in man pages (less) is efficient

additional_notes.navigation: Man pages use less pager - arrow keys, /search, n/N for next/prev, q to quit, h for help
additional_notes.sections: Man pages organized into sections: 1=commands, 2=system calls, 3=functions, 5=file formats, 8=admin
additional_notes.builtins: Shell built-ins (cd, history) don't have man pages - use help command instead
additional_notes.vs_info: info pages are alternative documentation format (more detailed but less common than man)
additional_notes.installation: Some man pages need to be installed: sudo apt install manpages manpages-dev
